read.sections.0.heading.back: A clue from inside the ground

read.sections.0.text.source: Ban Chiang is a village in northeast Thailand. Under it is a low hill, or mound, built up by people who lived there long ago. Archaeologists have found pottery, graves and metal objects there. UNESCO says the people of Ban Chiang farmed rice and knew how to make bronze, a metal, very early. These people left no writing, so objects are our main clues. A pot is an artefact: an object that people made or used. We can observe its shape and its painted marks. We cannot see what its maker thought, or every way people used it.
read.sections.0.text.back: Ban Chiang is a village in northeast Thailand. Under it is a low hill, or mound of earth, formed by people who lived there long ago. Archaeologists have found pottery, graves and metal objects there. UNESCO says that the people of Ban Chiang grew rice and knew how to make bronze, a kind of metal, at a very early time. They left no writing, so objects are our main clues. A pot is an artefact: an object made or used by people. We can observe its shape and the painted marks on it. We cannot see what its maker thought, or every way people used it.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: Ban Chiang is a village in Thailand. Under it is a low hill of earth. People lived there long ago. Archaeologists found pots, graves and metal things there. The people grew rice. They made bronze, a kind of metal. They left no writing. So objects are our clues. A pot is an artefact. People made it and used it. We can see its shape. We cannot see what the maker thought.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: Ban Chiang is a village in Thailand. Under it is a low hill of earth. People lived there long ago. Archaeologists found pottery, graves and metal things there. The people there grew rice. They made bronze, a kind of metal. They left no writing. So objects are our clues. A pot is an artefact. People made it and used it. We can see its shape. We cannot see what its maker thought.

read.sections.1.heading.back: Why the place of a find matters

read.sections.1.text.source: In 1974 and 1975, the Penn Museum in the United States and Thailand's Fine Arts Department dug at Ban Chiang. This careful digging and recording is called an excavation. The team recorded each find's context: where it lay in the ground and what was near it. Artists drew plans, which look down on the site, and sections, which show the layers from the side. Ban Chiang was a village and also a burial place. The layers were not always neat, and one layer could hold signs of both. So a pot found in a grave raises different questions from a pot found near a house.
read.sections.1.text.back: In 1974 and 1975, the Penn Museum in the United States and Thailand's Fine Arts Department dug at Ban Chiang. This careful work of digging and recording is called an excavation. The team recorded the context of each find: where it lay in the ground and what was near it. Artists drew plans, which show the site from above, and cross-sections, which show the layers of earth from the side. Ban Chiang was a village and also a burial place. Its layers were not always neat, and one layer could contain signs of both. So a pot found in a grave raises different questions from a pot found near a house.
read.sections.1.text.note: "Plans" and "sections" (archaeological drawings) are "pelan" and "keratan rentas". In Malay "pelan" means a drawn plan, which is right here.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: In 1974 and 1975, teams from Thailand and the United States dug at Ban Chiang. This careful digging is called an excavation. The teams wrote down the context of each find. That means where it was in the ground, and what was near it. People lived at Ban Chiang. People were buried there too. The layers were not always neat. A pot from a grave makes us ask different questions.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: In 1974 and 1975, teams from Thailand and the United States dug at Ban Chiang. This careful digging work is called an excavation. The team wrote down the context of each find. That means where the find was in the ground, and what was near it. People lived at Ban Chiang. People were also buried there. Its layers were not always neat. A pot from a grave makes us ask different questions.

read.sections.2.text.source: The second picture is a photo of one pot in a museum at Ban Chiang, taken in 2013. Start with observations: things you can see, such as its shape and its painted swirls. Then make an inference: an idea that might explain what you see. For example, someone chose to decorate this pot, because the pattern is there. But the photo cannot tell us who made the pot or which layer it came from. A museum label or an excavation record could help. When new evidence appears, historians change their ideas. Even the dates for Ban Chiang have changed over time.
read.sections.2.text.back: The second picture is a photo of a pot in a museum at Ban Chiang, taken in 2013. watch.summary.source: This is a short film by UNESCO and NHK, a Japanese broadcaster. It is about the Ban Chiang site in northeast Thailand. UNESCO's description of the film makes some big claims. It says the site has the earliest evidence in the region of farming. It says the site also has the earliest evidence of making and using metal. Think about these claims as you watch. Words like "earliest" are claims, not observations. They depend on the evidence found so far. Researchers have changed the dates for Ban Chiang over time. So a careful viewer asks two questions. What evidence supports each claim? Could new evidence change it?

educatorNotes.0.source: Aim: learners separate an observation from a careful inference about one artefact, and say what its context could add. Evidence move: ask what the museum photo leaves out about the pot's excavation context (its layer, what lay near it, grave or house area). A sound answer gives an observation, a tentative inference with "might", and a specific source to look for. Invite "we don't know yet" as a good answer.
educatorNotes.0.back: Aim: learners tell apart an observation and a careful inference about one artefact, and say what its context could add. Evidence step: ask what the museum photo does not show about the pot's excavation context (its layer, what lay near it, grave or house area). A good answer gives one observation, one careful inference with "might", and one specific source to look for. Encourage "we don't know yet" as a good answer.

educatorNotes.1.source: Misconception to address: a museum display photo is not a photo of the object where it was found, and neither "all pots were for burial" nor "this pot belonged to a farmer" follows from it. Source caveats: avoid any "first ever" date; UNESCO says the site's dating has been adjusted as radiometric dating improved, and the 1995 Penn article (which the Penn Museum flags as a historical reference) gives older date ranges, so the lesson says only "more than 2,000 years ago". The photo is an example; nothing says which trench this pot came from.

The photo is only an example; nothing says which trench this pot came from.
